Debt: Macron considers convening Parliament at Versailles in January to enshrine a “golden rule” in the Constitution

According to La Tribune Dimanche, Emmanuel Macron is considering convening Congress at Versailles in January 2027 to write into the Constitution a return to balanced public finances within three years. The Élysée is not commenting. The RN and LR welcome the idea, in the middle of the Senate's review of the 2027 budget [1][2][4].

According to the weekly, as reported on Sunday 22 November by several media outlets, the head of state is considering bringing both chambers together in Congress at Versailles in January to vote on a budgetary “golden rule” [1][2][3].
The principle: set a target of bringing revenue and spending back into balance over three years, across all public finances, from the central government to local authorities [1][2].

Emmanuel Macron could revive a 2011 constitutional bill, passed by the National Assembly and the Senate but never definitively adopted: Nicolas Sarkozy halted the procedure during his re-election campaign [4][5].
That 2011 text created “framework laws for balancing public finances” covering at least three years, and imposed deadlines for submitting the central government and Social Security budgets [4].
Revising the Constitution requires either a referendum or a vote by Congress with at least three-fifths of parliamentarians in favour [2][4]. The Élysée has not commented on these reports [4].

Jordan Bardella (RN) is pleased that the president appears to be coming round to his demand; Bruno Retailleau (LR) says such a rule in the Constitution would be “a good thing” [1][3]. Marine Le Pen, however, believes the 2011 text is not as “well crafted” as the rule proposed by the RN [5].

Édouard Philippe and Gabriel Attal, candidates of the centrist bloc for 2027, also support a golden rule [5]. It would probably be the last major initiative of Emmanuel Macron, who leaves the Élysée in May [3].
The key takeaway: lacking a majority to pass its budgets, the executive is trying to impose discipline through the Constitution, which would also bind the next president [1][4].
The context is tense: on 4 November, MPs rejected the “revenue” part of the 2027 budget by 458 votes to none, so it was the government's original text that was sent to the Senate [6].

The Senate is debating this budget in plenary from 20 November to 9 December, according to its official calendar [7]. The vote on the whole bill is expected on 9 December, and a joint committee (seven MPs and seven senators) must then seek a compromise by 17 December [8].

The path remains narrow: gathering three-fifths of Parliament requires the agreement of part of the opposition, and Marine Le Pen is already hinting that the 2011 text would need reworking, which would mean new readings [4][5].

A golden rule won't change your tax bill tomorrow morning. But if it is adopted, every future government will have to present a plan to balance the books within three years: either less public spending, more revenue, or both.

news.2026-11-23-kospi-chute-fonds-stabil: Seoul, South Korea
South Korea
“Black Monday” in Seoul: the Kospi plunges more than 5% intraday after −5.2% on Friday, and the government revives a rescue fund unused since 2008

On Monday 23 November, the Seoul stock exchange went through a “Black Monday”. The Kospi lost as much as 5.41% intraday and fell below 4,600 points, dragged down by Samsung and SK Hynix, after −5.21% on Friday. The government is preparing a 10,760 billion won stabilisation fund, which Korea has not used since 2008 [3][6][8][9][13].
The Kospi opened sharply lower: it was down 2.73% at 4,736.98 points after half an hour of trading, according to Reuters. Samsung Electronics was then down 3.44% and SK Hynix 2.16% [2].
The fall deepened during the morning: −3.85% at 9:50 a.m., according to the daily Asiae, which speaks of a “Black Monday” [4], then −4.33% at 11:20 a.m. Foreign investors then turned sellers [1].

At its worst, the index lost as much as 5.41% [6]. It fell below 4,600 points, and even into the 4,500 range according to broadcaster SBS [3][14]. A “side-car”, a brake that briefly suspends sales by computer programs, was triggered [3][11].

The reliable sources consulted did not yet give the exact closing figure. On Friday 20 November, the Kospi had already fallen 5.21% to 4,869.96 points, its lowest in ten months [13][15]. The won stood at 1,346.5 to the dollar in late morning on Monday [1].
On Sunday 22 November, the government held an emergency meeting and began preparing the stock market stabilisation fund, worth 10,760 billion won, or about $8 billion [5][8].

Deputy Prime Minister Lee Hyung-il said it is a “preliminary check”, not yet a decision to inject the money [5]. The fund can be used “if necessary”, according to SBS [14]. It has not been used since 2008, 18 years ago [9][15].
Seoul is also easing limits on companies buying back their own shares for three months, and stepping up surveillance of illegal short selling [5][7][8].

The key takeaway: South Korea is one of the stock markets most exposed to doubts about artificial intelligence. Samsung and SK Hynix make the memory chips used in AI servers, and they carry a very heavy weight in the index. When Wall Street sells tech, Seoul follows, often harder [2][12].

The promise of a support fund did not calm worries about AI, Reuters notes [2]. Investors doubt that the huge sums, often borrowed, spent on data centres will pay off quickly enough, Al Jazeera sums up [12].
The decline is spectacular: in early September, the Kospi was above 6,950 points [10]. On Monday, it fell below 4,600 points, roughly a third lower [3]. In October alone, it had lost 17.11% [19].

The stabilisation fund is used to buy shares when nobody else wants to. The aim is not to push the market back up at all costs, but to prevent cascading forced sales, such as those by investors who bought on credit [5][9].

If you hold an “emerging markets” or “Asia” fund in your life insurance or your PEA, Korea and its chipmakers often carry a heavy weight in it. A day like Monday shows up directly. A government support fund can slow a fall, but it does not set the long-term price.

How it works: the “side-car” and the stabilisation fund

A stock exchange has two tools against panic. The first is automatic: the “side-car”. When index futures fall too fast, the Seoul exchange briefly blocks sell orders placed by computer programs. This breaks the domino effect of robots selling because others are selling [3]. The second tool is political: a pooled fund, financed by banks, insurers and public institutions, that buys shares when sellers dominate. On Monday, Seoul announced it was preparing its own, worth 10,760 billion won [5][8]. It reassures mainly by existing: a buyer of last resort is there.
Precedents: crashes and rescue funds in Seoul

In the middle of the financial crisis, Korea launches a stabilisation fund of about 500 billion won; on the day the money reaches the market, the Kospi jumps 5.8% [17]. According to the Korea JoongAng Daily, the fund reached 515 billion won, of which 103 billion was injected first, and the index gained 55.04 points to 1,003.73 [18].
Announcing a buyer of last resort can trigger an immediate rebound, but it did not stop the crisis from dragging on.

The Kospi falls 8.8% to 2,441.55 points, its biggest percentage drop since 24 October 2008, with trading halted for the first time since 2020, according to Reuters [16].

Libya: a Russian corvette hit by drones in the port of Benghazi as the Ukraine war spills into the Mediterranean

On Sunday 22 November, an explosion struck a Russian warship docked at the Benghazi naval base in eastern Libya. Eastern authorities suspect a drone attack; Libyan officials blame Ukraine, which is not commenting. A Maltese cargo ship was also targeted and the UN is calling for an investigation [1][2][4][5].

According to the eastern government, allied with Marshal Khalifa Haftar, the ship had stopped to take on fuel and supplies before returning to Russia [2]. Satellite imagery company Vantor identified it as a Russian navy corvette [3].
Libyan military sources name it as the Merkury [1][4]. At least four drones were intercepted and destroyed, and two hit the corvette [1]. The human toll remains unclear [1][3].
The same day, a Maltese-flagged commercial vessel was struck by a naval drone off Benghazi; the eastern navy rescued the crew [1][4].

Libyan officials speak of Ukrainian naval drones; Kyiv has not responded [4]. Newsweek cites an unconfirmed report attributing the operation to the Ukrainian security service (SBU) [7]. Moscow had not commented on Sunday [2].
The eastern government denounces a violation of Libyan sovereignty and a threat to maritime security, and promises legal and diplomatic action [2].

In Tripoli, Abdelhamid Dbeibah's Government of National Unity warns against the use of Libyan ports in foreign conflicts: hosting foreign forces outside any legal framework can draw these clashes onto Libyan soil [6].
The UN mission in Libya condemns the attacks, calls for an investigation and warns that the country must not become “a battlefield for foreign conflicts” [5].
The key takeaway: if Ukraine is indeed responsible, this is a strike on a Russian Black Sea Fleet vessel far from its bases, in an eastern Libyan port controlled by an ally of Moscow [6][7].

Libya remains split in two. In the east, Haftar cooperates with Moscow: troops of the “Africa Corps”, under Russian control, operate in the south and east of the country [6]. In the west, Kyiv and Tripoli reportedly signed a secret agreement in 2025 allowing a Ukrainian military presence, according to the press [6].
This is not an isolated strike: in March, the Russian LNG tanker Arctic Metagaz sank off Libya after an attack that Moscow blamed on Ukraine [8].
The central Mediterranean is a major route for oil and gas reaching Europe. Naval drone attacks on ships there, including a civilian cargo vessel, raise the risk for shipping and insurance [1][5].

Libya is a few hundred kilometres from Italy and supplies oil and gas to Europe. If the war between Russia and Ukraine takes hold there, the cost of insuring ships in the Mediterranean could climb, and with it part of the price of energy.

Spain: final week before the snap general election on 29 November; Sánchez dreams of an “epic comeback”, polls favour the right and Vox

Spaniards vote on Sunday 29 November, after Socialist Pedro Sánchez's housing plan collapsed in Parliament. The campaign enters its final week: a four-way debate is scheduled for Thursday 26. Private polls put Alberto Núñez Feijóo's People's Party in the lead, with or without a majority for the right and Vox [1][3][4].
This snap election was triggered by Parliament's rejection of Pedro Sánchez's housing aid plan, which the Catalan separatists of Junts opposed; the Prime Minister then dissolved both chambers [1].
The official campaign began at midnight on 13 November and ends on 27 November [1].

Pedro Sánchez opened it in Seville by calling for an “epic comeback” through a massive mobilisation of left-wing voters [1]. Alberto Núñez Feijóo launched his in Badalona, near Barcelona, calling the government a “criminal, lying and corrupt mafia” [1].
The only televised head-to-head, on 19 November, focused on corruption, housing and the cost of living [4]. The conservative outlet Brussels Signal believes Feijóo clearly dominated it [2].
A four-way debate is scheduled for 26 November [4].
According to Brussels Signal, all private polls give the People's Party (PP) and Vox a combined majority [3]; The Olive Press instead points to a narrow PP lead [4].
The key takeaway: Spain could change majority on Sunday, and the whole question is whether the right will need the far-right Vox to govern [1][3].

Housing is at the heart of the vote: it was the failure of Pedro Sánchez's plan on this issue that brought down his majority, and rents are among voters' top concerns, along with the cost of living [1][4].

The PP is banking on the record of Feijóo, former president of Galicia, against what it describes as the “collapse” of the Sánchez government [5]. Corruption was one of the central themes of the 19 November debate [4].
In Catalonia, a key region, regional parties such as Junts, whose vote brought down the housing plan, are fielding their own candidates against the major national parties [1][6].
Spain is a neighbour and a major economic partner of France. A change of majority in Madrid could alter its policy on housing and immigration and its positions in European debates.

Nepal: eight months after taking power, Balendra Shah, a critic of New Delhi, visits Modi to ask for $2 billion in aid

Nepalese Prime Minister Balendra Shah, known as “Balen”, arrived in New Delhi on Sunday 22 November for a two-day state visit, his first trip abroad since taking office in March. He meets Narendra Modi on Monday. Energy, air routes and economic aid are on the agenda [1][3][4].
Balendra Shah is visiting at the invitation of Narendra Modi. It is his first visit to India and his first bilateral trip abroad since becoming Prime Minister at the end of March 2026 [1][6].

He is leading a 34-member delegation, including his chief adviser Kumar Byanjankar, Finance Minister Swarnim Wagle and Foreign Minister Shisir Khanal [1]. He began by meeting India's top diplomat, Subrahmanyam Jaishankar [2].

On Monday 23 November, the two leaders are due to hold talks at Hyderabad House in New Delhi, then exchange agreements and hold a joint press conference [4]. Balendra Shah is also due to be received by Indian President Droupadi Murmu [1].
Kathmandu has proposed a $2 billion economic aid package. According to the Indian press, New Delhi could accept it in principle, but disburse it in stages, project by project [3].
Nepal is also seeking access to Indian airspace to open new air routes [3]. Trade, hydropower, cross-border links and post-flood reconstruction are also on the agenda [3][4].
An economic vision document, entitled “Samriddha Nepal, Samunnat Bharat” (“Prosperous Nepal, Advanced India”), could be adopted [3].
The key takeaway: Nepal, wedged between India and China, is testing its relationship with its big southern neighbour under its new leader [5].

The visit comes as relations between the two countries are strained. Balendra Shah has criticised New Delhi in the past, and observers are watching whether he can balance his ties with India and with China [5].
For Nepal, a landlocked Himalayan country, links with India, hydropower and access to airspace are concrete issues at the heart of the visit [1][3].
For India, the goal is to keep Kathmandu within its sphere. By tying its aid to specific projects, New Delhi wants to keep control over how the money is used [3].

Nepal may seem far away, but it sits at the heart of the rivalry between the two Asian giants, India and China. If you travel in the Himalayas, new air routes via India could also make the country easier to reach.

Hong Kong at a 19-month low: Chinese tech has lost more than a third since January, and AI stocks $1.7 trillion

On Monday 23 November, the Hong Kong stock exchange fell again, by as much as 1.8%, hitting its lowest level since April 2025. Chinese tech giants are leading the decline: their index has lost more than a third since January, and Chinese AI stocks have lost $1.7 trillion [1][6].
The Hang Seng index opened down 1.38% at 22,100.51 points [3]. Alibaba was down 3% at the open, according to The Standard [2].
At the session's low, the Hang Seng was down about 1.8% and hit its lowest level since April 2025, 19 months ago, according to the South China Morning Post [1].
The technology index, the Hang Seng Tech, lost as much as 3% and fell below 3,400 points. Since January, it has lost more than a third [1]. Tencent fell nearly 2% to a new low [1].
At midday, the Hang Seng had trimmed its loss to 0.64%, at around 22,267 points, and the Hang Seng Tech was down 1.09%, according to The Standard [8].
On Friday 20 November, the Hang Seng had already lost 1.89% to 22,410.80 points [4]. It was then 20% below its 29 January peak, the threshold for a “bear market” [5].
According to Investing.com, AI-linked Chinese stocks have lost $1.7 trillion in market value in this sell-off [6].

The decline is region-wide: South Korea, Taiwan, Hong Kong and mainland China all fell on Monday [7]. The MSCI Asia-Pacific index is close to a bear market, about 18% below its June peak, according to Bloomberg [9].

The key takeaway: Hong Kong is the showcase for China's digital giants. When doubts about AI hit Wall Street, these groups are hit twice: by fears that AI spending won't pay off enough, and by US restrictions on chips [6][11].

Investors doubt that China can keep developing its AI while Washington tightens the screws on the most advanced semiconductor technologies, Investing.com explains [6]. Business Today also cites fears of new US rules that would limit Chinese groups' access to computing power [11].

The move accelerated this week: the Hang Seng posted four straight sessions of losses through Friday [11]. It had already fallen to 22,841.62 points on the day of the summit between Donald Trump, Vladimir Putin and Xi Jinping [10].
A “bear market” doesn't mean the decline will stop or continue. It is a benchmark: a 20% fall from the peak. Above all, it signals that investor sentiment has shifted from buying to caution [5].

If you hold a “China” or “emerging markets” fund, Alibaba and Tencent are often among its largest holdings. Their fall of nearly half since the start of the year shows up in these funds. Diversifying across several regions limits the impact of any single market.

Gas: the cold is coming, Norway is delivering less and European storage is at its lowest in more than a decade; the price jumps nearly 5%

Gas prices in Europe are rising again as winter sets in. The benchmark TTF contract jumped 4.7% to €88.45 per megawatt-hour, with the arrival of cold weather and an outage in Norway. European storage is only about 70% full, compared with about 82% a year ago, and a “polar vortex” looms [1][3][9].
The TTF, Europe's benchmark gas price, traded in the Netherlands, rose 4.73% to €88.45 per megawatt-hour on 20 November, according to Trading Economics [3].
Trading Economics cites an outage at Norway's large Troll field, which is reducing gas deliveries to Europe [3].

On 16 November, European storage was 70.2% full, and Germany's about 57%, according to Engie's tracker [2]. On 19 November, the rate was about 70%, compared with about 82% a year earlier and a five-year average of 89% for this time of year [9].
According to CNBC, European stocks began the winter at their lowest level in more than a decade. David Lewis, of consultancy Wood Mackenzie, even calls it the lowest ever recorded [1].
Withdrawals from storage during the first half of November were among the largest ever seen, David Lewis adds [1].
The threat comes from the sky: an early collapse of the “polar vortex”, combined with a strong El Niño, raises the risk of a cold snap that would drain stocks even faster [1][7].
On Friday afternoon, the December contract was worth about €87.28, far from its peak of €103.9 at the end of October [1].

The key takeaway: in winter, Europe heats its homes by drawing on storage filled during the summer. The less gas there is at the start, the more strongly the price reacts to each cold snap or outage. That is the case this year [1][2].

Norway is a major pipeline supplier to Europe. A drop in its deliveries, as with the Troll outage, therefore shows up immediately in prices [3]. On top of this is the risk around the Strait of Hormuz, through which part of the Gulf's liquefied natural gas passes [6].

The polar vortex is a swirl of frigid air above the Arctic. When it is disrupted, this cold air can move down towards Europe for weeks. Combined with a strong El Niño, it raises fears of a harsher start to winter [1][7].
The gas price matters well beyond heating: it often sets the price of electricity in Europe and weighs on chemicals and heavy industry.

If your gas or electricity contract tracks market prices, a lasting rise in the TTF could show up on your bills in a few months. With a fixed price, you are protected until the end of the contract. Turning your heating down by one degree remains the simplest way to limit the impact.

How it works: why low storage sends gas prices soaring

Europe produces little gas. It fills its underground storage in summer, when demand is low, and draws it down in winter. The TTF price, traded in the Netherlands, reflects what buyers fear for the weeks ahead. When storage is well filled, a cold snap has little effect: there is a margin. When it is low, as this year with about 70% filled compared with about 82% a year earlier [9], every cold forecast or outage raises fears of a shortage at the end of winter. Buyers then hedge earlier, and the price rises fast: +4.73% in a single day on 20 November [3].
Precedents: a year of gas under strain
August 2022
After the war in Ukraine and the cut in Russian deliveries, TTF contracts close at a record €339 per megawatt-hour, according to Euronews [10]; Argus records a high of €319 on 26 August 2022 [11].
The current price, around €88, remains far from that record: the market fears tightness, not yet a shortage.
Summer 2026
European storage is only about 63% full, its lowest level for the season in nearly twenty years, according to Oilprice [4].
The shortfall built up over the summer was never made up: Europe enters winter with storage at about 70%, compared with an 89% average [9].

As a first cold snap approaches, the TTF tops €97 per megawatt-hour [5], then reaches a peak of €103.9 [1].
Prices come back down when the cold passes: in early November, the TTF moved away from €100 [8].

European gas prices jump on risks around the Strait of Hormuz, which disrupt flows, according to Tradingpedia [6].
European gas now depends as much on the weather as on Middle East geopolitics.

Part of the trade between Asia and the east coast of the Americas passes through this canal: these tensions could weigh on shipping costs.
